newsitem.title: BOSNIA: West gives cautious reaction to Mladic's dismissal.
newsitem.headline: West gives cautious reaction to Mladic's dismissal.

text.p: NATO and Western mediators said on Saturday they would "wait and see" if Bosnian Serb leaders were able to carry out a decision to dismiss Serb army chief Ratko Mladic, an accused war criminal.
"We don't know what it is going to mean in substantive terms until the next couple of days have played out," Major Simon Haselock, spokesman for the NATO-led peace force, told a news conference.
Haselock spoke after Bosnian Serb President Biljana Plavsic announced she had replaced Mladic and other top generals "due to the international community's well-known stand".
The Dayton peace agreement requires Mladic and other indicted war criminals to step down from public office and face trial before a U.N. tribunal. He has so far refused to comply.
Haselock said NATO was still trying to confirm whether the Bosnian Serb army -- which has been locked in a long-running dispute with its civilian authorities -- would obey Plavsic's order.
"As of this moment however we have not received any official notification of changes (in the military leadership)," he said.
"Of course we expect to maintain our usual contacts up and down and throughout the chain of the command."
Another U.S. embassy official who asked not to be named described the news as "a good first step that should have been taken a long time ago".
A spokesman for the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carl Bildt, said it was too early to tell the outcome of the power struggle between civilian and military leaders.
"(Bildt) thinks it's a little premature and is waiting to see what comes out of this particular move by Madame Plavsic," Murphy said.
"We've seen similar moves in the past."

Former Bosnian Serb president Radovan Karadzic, also indicted by the U.N. war crimes tribunal, tried to sack Mladic and a number of top generals last year but the army rejected his order, and the officers remained in place.
During the Bosnian war, Serb army officers accused Karadzic's cabinet of war profiteering and depriving the military of valuable resources.
Bosnian Serb politicians accused the officers of taking orders exclusively from the Belgrade government in neighbouring Serbia, which funded the army.
Radio Netherlands quoted an interview with Mladic's deputy General Manojlo Milovanovac in which he reportedly rejected Plavsic's decree as meaningless, and said the army would resist the move.
"Only the parliament can sack him (Mladic)," Milovanovac said. "Nothing has changed (to Mladic's position), and nothing will change."
Plavsic's statement indicated she had sacked most of the army's general staff, including Milovanovac, and named an obscure officer, General Pera Colic, as chief of a new army headquarters.
The announcement also followed weeks of speculation in Belgrade media which predicted Mladic's retirement and cast doubt on his health.
NATO sources said they had few contacts with Colic and that he had not played a prominent leadership role in the army thus far.
An adviser to the Moslem chairman of the collective presidency, Alija Izetbegovic, said Plavsic's move was a positive step but fell short of full compliance with the Dayton agreement.
Mladic and Karadzic have been indicted for crimes against humanity and genocide linked to the siege of Sarajevo, the capture of U.N. peacekeepers and the massacre of Moslems from Srebrenica.
